analyst:
Texas Tech enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 22-9 overall and 12-6 in Big 12 play, earning a No. 5 seed in the Midwest Region and drawing No. 12 Akron on Friday, March 20, 2026. The official Texas Tech schedule shows the Red Raiders closed the regular season with losses to TCU on March 3 and at BYU on March 7, then lost 75-53 to Iowa State in the Big 12 Tournament quarterfinal on March 12. The same schedule page lists the NCAA opener against Akron and confirms the 22-9, 12-6 baseline entering the bracket. Texas Tech’s best résumé wins were 90-86 over No. 6 Houston on January 24, 78-75 in overtime at No. 1 Arizona on February 14, and 82-73 at No. 4 Iowa State on February 28. Those are not abstract “good wins”; they show Tech can beat elite teams both at home and on the road. 

Offensively, Texas Tech under Grant McCasland is built around spacing, ball movement, and a high-volume three-point attack that still runs through an interior star. Texas Tech’s own game notes reported the Red Raiders had already produced 16 games with 10 or more made threes by mid-February, were averaging 17.0 assists per game, and had logged multiple 20-assist games, including 23 assists on 30 made field goals at Oklahoma State and 24 assists on 34 makes at Utah. That profile matters on film: Tech is not a stagnant post-up team even though JT Toppin is its best player. The ball is driven inside-out through Toppin duck-ins, short-roll catches, and offensive rebounding, then kicked to shooters like Christian Anderson and Donovan Atwell. In the overtime road win at Arizona on February 14, Tech got 31 points and 13 rebounds from Toppin, 19 points and 8 assists from Anderson, and 11 points from Atwell on 3-of-9 from three. That box score is the cleanest snapshot of their preferred formula: a dominant scoring 4/5, a primary creator guard, and secondary spacing from the wings. Against Kansas on February 2, Tech attempted 40 threes and only 5 free throws in a 64-61 loss, with Donovan Atwell going 4-of-13 from deep and Jaylen Petty 3-of-9; that game showed the downside of the offense when Tech settles and cannot balance perimeter volume with paint pressure. 

The specific tendency to watch is that Tech will play through Toppin early, but late-clock possessions often shift to Anderson ball screens and drive-kick decisions. ESPN’s team leaders page lists Toppin at 21.8 points and 10.8 rebounds per game, while Anderson leads the team in assists at 7.7 per game. That statistical split tracks the eye test: Toppin is the finisher, Anderson the organizer. Tech’s assist rate and repeated double-digit three-point games show a real commitment to sharing the ball, not just freelancing. In blowout wins, the spacing becomes overwhelming: Texas Tech beat Kansas State 100-72 on February 21 and Cincinnati 80-68 on February 24, then won at Iowa State 82-73 on February 28. The Kansas State game is especially revealing because Tech reached 100 with balanced pace and shot creation rather than one player hijacking possessions. 

Defensively, McCasland’s group still carries traditional Texas Tech traits: hard ball pressure, physical rebounding, and a preference for forcing opponents into a contested half-court game. The clearest evidence is in the scores and shot-volume suppression. Texas Tech held Colorado to 44 points on February 11 in a 78-44 win, held West Virginia to 63 on February 8, and held Cincinnati to 68 on February 24. In the win at Arizona, Tech survived despite Arizona’s bench edge because it kept the Wildcats to 25.0 percent from three and won the overtime segment 12-9. In the loss to Kansas, Tech forced the Jayhawks to 30.0 percent from three, but Kansas still won because Tech allowed 38 rebounds and got crushed in paint efficiency relative to its own 31.9 percent overall shooting night. The March 12 loss to Iowa State is the warning sign for tournament opponents: Iowa State scored 42 points in the paint, 17 points off turnovers, and shot 53.6 percent overall, while Tech managed only 33.9 percent from the field and just 18 paint points. When Tech’s first line is broken and it cannot finish possessions with rebounds, the defense stops looking like a lockdown unit. 

McCasland’s coaching philosophy is visible in how often Texas Tech changes game texture across 40 minutes. His teams do not mind playing fast if the ball is moving, but they are comfortable winning grinder games too. The January 24 Houston win is a documented example of in-game adaptation: Houston scored 49 first-half points, but Tech still won 90-86 by matching shot-making and refusing to let the game become a purely physical slog. The February 14 Arizona win is an even stronger adjustment example. Texas Tech was tied 32-32 at halftime and then won overtime on the road behind Toppin’s eight points in the extra session; that indicates McCasland successfully re-centered the offense through his star after a balanced first half. By contrast, the March 3 loss to TCU showed the vulnerability when the adjustment fails: Tech led 39-36 at halftime but scored only 26 after the break in a 73-65 defeat. Against BYU on March 7, Tech led 46-38 at halftime and still lost 82-76, another case where second-half counters were not enough. Those two March games are important because they show recent slippage against physical or shot-making opponents who survive the initial Tech punch. 

Late-game execution has been mostly strong against top competition. Texas Tech beat Houston 90-86 on January 24, beat Colorado 73-71 on January 10, and won at Arizona 78-75 in overtime on February 14. The Arizona game is the headline clutch example: on the road, against the No. 1 team in the country, Toppin finished with 31 and 13, Anderson added 19 and 8 assists, and Tech won the extra period 12-9. The Houston result also matters because it came against a veteran, physical team and Tech still reached 90. On the other side, the February 2 Kansas loss was a failed late-game execution test; Tech lost 64-61 at home despite taking 72 shots, because 23-of-72 overall and 3-of-5 at the line left no margin. The March 3 TCU loss is another concern point because Tech had the home floor, led at half, and was outscored 37-26 after intermission. 

The key players start with JT Toppin, the All-America level frontcourt anchor. ESPN lists him at 21.8 points, 10.8 rebounds, 1.4 steals, and 1.7 blocks per game. His standout moments are major and recent: 31 points and 13 rebounds in the February 14 win at Arizona, 41 points and 15 rebounds in the 111-106 double-overtime win over Arizona State on February 12, 32 points and 12 rebounds at Oklahoma State, and 30 points with 14 rebounds in the home finale against Colorado according to Texas Tech game notes. Christian Anderson is the lead guard and offensive connector; ESPN lists him at 7.7 assists per game, and in the Arizona win he posted 19 points with 8 assists while playing 45 minutes. Donovan Atwell is the key floor-spacer; he scored 11 against Arizona on 3-of-9 from three and 12 against Kansas on 4-of-13 from deep. LeJuan Watts gives Tech another physical wing rebounder and secondary creator; in the Kansas loss he had 19 points and 12 rebounds, showing he can be a pressure release when Toppin is crowded. Jaylen Petty’s value is as a complementary guard who can move the ball and defend multiple spots; he had 11 points and 7 assists against Kansas even in defeat. 

The notable wins tell you Texas Tech’s ceiling. The 90-86 win over No. 6 Houston on January 24 revealed that Tech can win a high-level physical game without losing its offensive identity. The 78-75 overtime win at No. 1 Arizona on February 14 revealed real March toughness, because Tech took a road punch, got a superstar game from Toppin, and executed in overtime. The 82-73 win at No. 4 Iowa State on February 28 revealed resilience after a rough mid-February stretch and showed Tech could win in one of the league’s hardest road environments. The notable losses show the pressure points. The 64-61 home loss to Kansas on February 2 revealed that three-point volume can become over-reliance when the offense does not manufacture free throws. The 73-65 home loss to TCU on March 3 and 82-76 loss at BYU on March 7 revealed second-half fragility entering the tournament. The 75-53 Big 12 Tournament loss to Iowa State on March 12 was the worst data point of all: only 53 points, only 18 paint points, and 10 turnovers while allowing Iowa State to shoot 53.6 percent. 

As for McCasland’s NCAA Tournament history, Texas Tech’s official coaching bio says he led North Texas to the 2020-21 NCAA Tournament Round of 32, highlighted by the program’s first NCAA Tournament win, and Texas Tech materials entering the 2025 postseason note he had already taken the Red Raiders to back-to-back NCAA Tournaments in his first two seasons. Texas Tech’s 2025 season review states the Red Raiders reached the 2025 Elite Eight under McCasland, while his first Texas Tech team in 2024 reached the NCAA Tournament but exited in the first round. So his documented Division I NCAA head-coaching history includes the 2021 Round of 32 at North Texas, a 2024 First Round appearance at Texas Tech, and a 2025 Elite Eight at Texas Tech. 

Bottom line: Texas Tech is a dangerous, traditional March team because it has the two ingredients that travel — an elite interior star in JT Toppin and a defense capable of dragging games into half-court possessions. But the volatility is real. If Anderson controls tempo and Toppin touches the paint every trip, Tech looks like a second-weekend team. If the offense becomes a jump-shot diet like it did in the Kansas loss or gets physically dislodged like it did against Iowa State in the Big 12 Tournament, the upset path opens immediately.

Texas Tech enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a profile that is stronger on underlying quality than some surface-level narratives suggest. As of Selection Sunday week, the Red Raiders were 22-10 overall, tied for third in the Big 12 at 12-6, earned the No. 4 seed in the Big 12 Tournament, and finished No. 19 in the NCAA NET rankings. ESPN’s BPI page placed Texas Tech 13th nationally, while public reporting through late January and February repeatedly had the Red Raiders operating in or around the national top 10-to-20 band, including a No. 16 AP ranking entering the Big 12 Tournament. ([ncaa.com](https://www.ncaa.com/rankings/basketball-men/d1/ncaa-mens-basketball-net-rankings))

The most important macro takeaway is that this is not a classic Texas Tech team built purely on drag-you-into-the-mud defense. The statistical shape is much more offense-forward than the old Chris Beard-era stereotype. ESPN team totals show Texas Tech averaging 80.4 points per game while shooting 46.7% from the field and 39.3% from three. Across 32 games, the Red Raiders made 369 threes on 938 attempts, a 39.3% clip, while producing 2,573 total points on 3,780 field-goal attempts and 529 free-throw attempts. Those raw totals translate to an estimated team effective field-goal percentage of 56.5%, a very strong mark, and a 3-point attempt rate of 24.8% when measured as 3PA/FGA from the available team totals. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2641))

Using the same team-total data, Texas Tech’s estimated turnover rate comes out to just 8.6%, which is elite ball security by any standard. Their estimated offensive rebounding rate is 31.2%, and their estimated free-throw rate is 0.140. That combination paints a very specific offensive identity: this is a shotmaking team first, not a pure rim-pressure or glass-crash machine. They protect possessions exceptionally well, space the floor, and win with accuracy and execution more than with foul-drawing volume. In other words, the Red Raiders’ offense looks more like a modern skill-and-decision offense than a brute-force one. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2641))

Personnel data reinforces that read. Christian Anderson was the engine, averaging 19.2 points and 7.8 assists per game in regular-season reporting, leading the Big 12 in assists and ranking third nationally in assists per game according to Texas Tech’s March 11 tournament notes. Donovan Atwell gave them major perimeter gravity, and Texas Tech’s own release noted that the team had made 360 threes by that point, already the second-most in school history. JT Toppin was an interior star before his season-ending ACL injury in mid-February; before that, ESPN’s season stats page listed him at 21.8 points and 10.8 rebounds per game. ([texastech.com](https://texastech.com/news/2026/3/11/mens-basketball-tech-iowa-state-set-for-big-12-tournament-quarterfinals))

That injury matters enormously in any tournament forecast. It changes the way we should interpret both full-season efficiency and late-season trend. Before Toppin went down, Texas Tech had the profile of a high-end Big 12 contender with top-tier shotmaking balance inside and out. After the injury, the team’s style necessarily shifted more toward spacing, Anderson’s creation, and Atwell’s shooting. Yet the results immediately after the loss were more resilient than expected: NCAA.com reported that Texas Tech beat Iowa State on February 28 for its fourth win over an AP top-6 opponent and improved to 3-0 since losing Toppin. That is exactly the kind of result set that suggests the market and conventional wisdom may underrate the remaining roster. ([ncaa.com](https://www.ncaa.com/news/basketball-men/article/2026-02-28/no-16-texas-tech-upsets-no-4-iowa-state-82-73-fourth-ap-top-6-win?utm_source=openai))

Recent form, though, was not linear. Texas Tech closed the regular season with a notable home loss to TCU on March 3, falling 73-65 after entering on a three-game winning streak since Toppin’s injury. Then, in the Big 12 Tournament quarterfinals on March 12, the Red Raiders were handled 75-53 by Iowa State, a game in which Anderson also strained a muscle after slipping on the floor. So the last-10-games story is mixed: there was a strong post-Toppin bounce that showed schematic adaptability and shotmaking resilience, but the immediate pre-tournament snapshot included two clear offensive downturns against NCAA-caliber opponents. That suggests their rolling efficiency trend was probably positive in the first phase after the injury, then dipped sharply entering the field. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/401827719?utm_source=openai))

On tempo, exact public possession-based pace numbers were not readily accessible in the open sources returned here, but the statistical texture suggests Texas Tech is not an extreme pace team. They score efficiently enough to post 80.4 points per game, but the profile is driven more by shooting efficiency and low turnovers than by obvious volume inflation. In practical terms, this looks like a controlled-possession offense rather than a pure transition machine. The best synthesis from the available data is that Texas Tech likely sits around the national middle or slightly above it in pace, while creating offensive value through half-court precision. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2641))

Strength of schedule is implied more than explicitly quantified in the public pages available here, but the Big 12 context is itself a major indicator. Texas Tech finished 12-6 in a league that placed multiple teams near the top of the NET and BPI ecosystems, and their résumé line in the NET page shows meaningful high-end competition: 5-5 in Quadrant 1 and 3-3 in Quadrant 2, with a strong 14-2 mark outside those bands. That is a serious tournament résumé, not a padded win-loss record. Their four wins over AP top-6 opponents, as cited by NCAA.com in late February, further emphasize that the ceiling was real. ([ncaa.com](https://www.ncaa.com/rankings/basketball-men/d1/ncaa-mens-basketball-net-rankings))

Where do the numbers diverge from the eye test? First, Texas Tech’s brand still cues “defense-first rock fight,” but the actual 2025-26 profile is much more offensive and perimeter-skilled. Second, losing Toppin should have cratered them; instead, they initially showed surprising elasticity because Anderson’s playmaking and Atwell’s shooting preserved a high-level offensive framework. Third, the raw scoring average may cause some analysts to assume pace-driven offense, but the deeper signal from the available data is surgical efficiency: strong eFG%, absurdly low turnover rate, and elite lead-guard creation. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2641))

The caution flag is equally clear. If Anderson is limited after the March 12 muscle strain, then Texas Tech loses the one element that made the post-Toppin version viable: high-end on-ball orchestration. Without Toppin’s interior scoring and with any reduction in Anderson’s burst or minutes, the offense can flatten quickly, as the 53-point outing against Iowa State showed. So the true tournament answer is bifurcated. Full-season data says Texas Tech is the profile of a dangerous second-weekend-quality team: top-20 NET, top-15-ish BPI, elite ball security, strong shooting, proven wins. Immediate pre-tournament context says they are more fragile than those season-long numbers imply because the roster is now much narrower and more dependent on perimeter creators being fully healthy. ([ncaa.com](https://www.ncaa.com/rankings/basketball-men/d1/ncaa-mens-basketball-net-rankings))

Bottom line: Texas Tech’s 2026 statistical identity is that of a high-skill, low-turnover, shotmaking-heavy Big 12 power whose offense is better than the program stereotype, whose résumé quality is real, and whose tournament volatility is driven almost entirely by health. If healthy enough in the backcourt, the Red Raiders are underseed-style dangerous because the public may still think of them as a defense brand. The data says the real edge is offensive efficiency, decision quality, and shot conversion.
matchup-analyst:
Texas Tech enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a team whose identity is built on spacing, shotmaking, and high-level lead-guard orchestration. Through March 1, the Red Raiders were 22-7, averaging 82.0 points per game while allowing 72.2, and they had already made 287 threes through 25 games by mid-February while leading the Big 12 at 11.5 made threes per game and ranking second in the league at 38.9% from three. Christian Anderson is the engine: by March 7 he was averaging 19.1 points and 7.7 assists per game while shooting 42.4% from three, and Donovan Atwell had 115 made threes, with Anderson at 97 entering the regular-season finale. That tells you exactly what the offense wants: Anderson probing, kickout chains, and a barrage of catch-and-shoot threes around a star frontcourt scorer in JT Toppin before Toppin’s season-ending ACL tear on February 17. ([texastech.com](https://texastech.com/documents/download/2026/3/1/Tech__22-7_.pdf))

Style of play: Tech is most dangerous when it can create rhythm threes early in possessions and play from advantage after Anderson collapses the first line. The best evidence is its ceiling games. Against Oklahoma State on January 3, Texas Tech matched a program record with 17 made threes in a 102-80 win, with Anderson posting 19 points and 13 assists. Against Baylor on January 20, Tech again hit 17 threes and set a Big 12 record with 14 first-half threes in a 92-73 road win. Against Houston on January 24, Tech scored 90 and led 55-49 at halftime after going 10-for-19 from three in the first half. Those games show the formula: spread floor, fast decisions, multiple shooters on the arc, and Anderson dictating tempo and distribution. ([texastech.com](https://texastech.com/news/2026/1/3/mens-basketball-no-15-red-raiders-roll-in-big-12-opener?utm_source=openai))

The specific tactics that disrupt this offense are equally clear. First, extended ball pressure that turns Anderson’s initiation into a survival possession matters. In the February 17 loss at Arizona State, ESPN’s recap said ASU’s full-court press “forced multiple turnovers,” and McCasland said the decisive stat was Tech’s “inability to take care of the ball which led to some transition baskets.” Texas Tech’s season high in turnovers through March 1 was 17, and that came in that Arizona State game. Second, physical switching and late-clock shot denial work when the threes dry up: in the February 2 loss to Kansas, Tech scored only 61, shot 23-for-72 overall and just 12-for-40 from three, and managed only 0.85 points per shot per FOX’s game log. Third, size-and-rebounding pressure without Toppin changes the team dramatically: in the March 3 loss to TCU, Tech was out-rebounded 39-25, lost the offensive glass 16-7, and was outscored 38-22 in the paint. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/401827686?utm_source=openai))

Press and zone vulnerability: there is direct evidence on press vulnerability and indirect-but-usable evidence on zone-style disruption. The clearest press example is Arizona State on February 17, where the full-court press created turnovers and transition scores in a 72-67 Tech loss. A second pressure example is TCU on March 3: while not explicitly labeled a press-heavy game, TCU forced 15 turnovers and converted them into an 18-11 edge in points off turnovers, which is the exact profile of a defense that sped Tech up and broke offensive flow. On zone or packed-lane looks, Kansas is the best practical example of what bothers Tech: Tech attempted 40 threes but made only 12 and scored just 61 points, suggesting Kansas successfully walled off cleaner interior creation and forced a lower-efficiency jump-shot diet. Purdue is the extreme version of this problem: Tech scored a season-low 56 in the November 21 neutral-court loss, its fewest points of the year through March 1. Even without full possession-type data from Synergy publicly accessible here, the named games show the structural weakness: if you flatten Anderson’s first touch and force Tech into static, over-the-top jump shooting, the offense becomes much easier to guard. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/401827686?utm_source=openai))

Preferred pace and how to force the opposite: Tech’s preferred game is not reckless speed; it is controlled offensive rhythm with enough tempo to find early threes before the defense gets set. Their best offensive games came when they could score in the 80s or 90s with low turnover counts, such as Houston on January 24 with only eight turnovers and Baylor on January 20 with elite early shooting. To force the opposite, make the game uglier and more physical. Kansas dragged Tech into a 64-61 grinder. Arizona State made them play through pressure and broken floor balance. TCU turned the contest into a rebounding-and-turnover fight. If you can deny clean first-side threes, send the ball to Tech’s secondary creators, and make them finish over set interior size, you pull them away from their comfort zone. The post-Toppin version is especially vulnerable to that because the elite release valve on the block is gone. ([texastech.com](https://texastech.com/news/2026/1/24/mens-basketball-no-12-texas-tech-knocks-off-no-6-houston?utm_source=openai))

Size and athleticism mismatches by position: at point guard, Anderson is 6-3/178, so bigger, physical lead guards can bump him and wear on him over 40 minutes. At the wings, Atwell and Tyeree Bryan are both 6-5, giving Tech good positional size, but they are more dangerous as shooters than downhill power drivers. LeJuan Watts is 6-6/225 and can bully smaller wings, but against true high-major fours his size is only adequate. The frontcourt is where the scouting changed most. Toppin, a 6-9/230 forward, was the dominant mismatch piece at 21.8 points and 10.8 rebounds per game before his ACL tear, but without him Tech relies more heavily on Luke Bamgboye at 6-11/220 and Marial Akuentok at 6-11/240. Bamgboye gives length but got into foul trouble against TCU; Akuentok provides bulk but had played sparingly. That means opponent scouting should target Tech at the 4 and 5: post seals, offensive rebounding, and foul pressure on Bamgboye matter much more now than they did when Toppin was available. ([texastech.com](https://texastech.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster))

Isolation versus team offense tendencies: the available public evidence points strongly toward a team-offense lean rather than a pure isolation attack. Texas Tech averaged 17.0 assists per game in a February team report, and Anderson alone was at 7.7 assists per game by early March. In their best games, the assist totals spike: 24 assists against Utah, 22 against Wake Forest, and Anderson had 13 assists against Oklahoma State. That is not the profile of an iso-heavy team. Their offense is much more drive-kick-swing than clear-a-side isolation, though Anderson can take late-clock creation reps and Toppin previously gave them a one-on-one scoring option inside. Because exact Synergy isolation-play percentages are not publicly surfaced in the accessible sources here, the most defensible conclusion is this: Texas Tech’s actual shot creation is led by advantage basketball and ball movement, and when opponents force them into late-clock individual creation, efficiency drops, as seen in the Kansas and Arizona State losses. ([texastech.com](https://texastech.com/news/2025/2/16/mens-basketball-red-raider-report-game-26?utm_source=openai))

Transition offense and defense frequency: direct frequency percentages are not publicly available in the accessible sources, but the game evidence is still actionable. McCasland explicitly said Arizona State converted Tech turnovers into transition baskets, which means Tech’s transition defense can be attacked when its ball security fails. Conversely, Tech’s offense is devastating when turnovers stay low and made threes let them play from ahead; against Houston they had only eight turnovers in a 90-point outing, and against Baylor they created such an early avalanche that the game became a flow contest on Tech’s terms. The practical scouting takeaway is that Tech is not a pure run-and-gun transition team; rather, transition becomes a multiplier for them off live-ball events and early-clock kick-ahead threes. If you keep your own turnover rate low and make them play against a set half-court shell, you remove a major source of their momentum offense. ([texastech.com](https://texastech.com/news/2026/2/18/mens-basketball-no-13-tech-falls-at-arizona-state))

Coaching adaptability: yes, McCasland’s staff has shown real in-game adjustment capability. The strongest named example is BYU on January 17, when Texas Tech rallied from a 61-52 deficit with 9:26 left by unleashing a 30-6 run to win 84-71. That is not random variance; that is a staff changing coverage, tempo, and shot quality midgame. Another data point is that Tech was 20-2 in games it led at halftime entering March 3, which suggests the staff usually protects advantages effectively. There is also evidence of situational resilience after losses: after the Kansas collapse on February 2, Tech went on the road and beat West Virginia 70-63; after the Arizona State upset and Toppin injury, Tech still beat Kansas State, Cincinnati, and Iowa State before stumbling late. ([thescore.com](https://www.thescore.com/ncaab/events/2458041/RECAP?utm_source=openai))

Concrete game plan: To beat this team you must do five things. First, pick up Anderson full court and make every catch start two steps farther from the arc; Arizona State proved this can work. Second, top-lock and chase the shooters, especially Atwell and Anderson, off the line; Tech’s offensive ceiling games are all three-point barrages. Third, attack the offensive glass and the paint, especially now that Toppin is out; TCU’s 39-25 rebounding edge and 38-22 paint edge is the template. Fourth, make Tech finish through contact without living at the line or in clean catch-and-shoot rhythm; Kansas held them to 61 and Purdue held them to 56. Fifth, keep your own live-ball turnovers down, because Tech becomes much more manageable in a pure half-court game than in a game where Anderson is spraying early threes in flow. In one sentence: pressure Anderson, run shooters off the line, punish the post-Toppin frontcourt on the glass, and force Texas Tech to win with contested twos instead of assisted threes. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/401827686?utm_source=openai))
